hypothesis: The taxonomic similarity of marine fossil faunas from two geological stages decreases with the time separating them, consecutive stages being far more similar than widely separated ones, and the fauna of each stage is intermediate between the faunas of the stages before and after it.
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. Using Paleobiology Database marine Metazoa genus lists per international stage (ICS 2020 scale as served by PBDB; stages shorter than 1 Myr excluded; stages with fewer than 200 genera excluded), compute Jaccard similarity between all stage pairs. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the Spearman correlation between pairwise Jaccard similarity and the separation of stage midpoints (Myr) is <= -0.5 with Mantel permutation p < 0.001, (ii) the mean Jaccard similarity of consecutive stage pairs is at least 2 times the mean similarity of pairs separated by 5 or more intervening stages, and (iii) for at least 80% of stages i with both neighbours, J(i-1, i+1) <= min(J(i-1, i), J(i, i+1)) (intermediacy).
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the Spearman correlation is > -0.2, or the consecutive/remote similarity ratio is < 1.2, or intermediacy holds for fewer than 50% of stages. Other outcomes are 'mixed'.
interpretation: Darwin's 'formations' are read as international chronostratigraphic stages (the finest global units with ages), 'fossils ... closely related' as sharing of genera (the finest rank that is comparable across regions in PBDB), and 'remote' as separation by five or more stages. 'Intermediate' is read as: two stages bracketing a third never share more genera with each other than either shares with the middle stage. Only marine environments are used because marine faunas have the most continuous record. Modern reinterpretation: PBDB stage assignments of collections rest partly on biostratigraphy, which could inflate within-stage faunal homogeneity; the pass criterion therefore requires a large, graded effect over multi-stage separations, not merely a within-stage one.
